meaning: The size of King Uzziah's army: 307,500 fighting men
description: The number 307,500 indicates the exact count of soldiers in King Uzziah's army, as described in 2 Chronicles 26:13. This mighty army was under the command of 2,600 family heads and fought with great strength to help the king against his enemies. The army testifies to Uzziah's enormous military power and Judah's golden age during his reign. The books of Chronicles emphasize that Uzziah's success was directly linked to his reverence for God: "As long as he sought the Lord, God gave him success" (2 Chron 26:5). The precise figure of 307,500 reflects the biblical historians' emphasis on accurate documentation of military resources and highlights how God's blessing manifested in tangible strength for His chosen people. Nevertheless, the account also contains a warning: the same king who enjoyed such blessing fell when pride took hold.

footnotes.text: King Uzziah (also called Azariah) reigned over Judah for about 52 years (c. 792–740 BC) and was one of the longest-reigning kings. His reign represented one of Judah's most prosperous periods.
The 2,600 family heads who led the army (2 Chron 26:12) formed the command structure. With 307,500 soldiers, this averages about 118 men per family head.

The detailed military figures in Chronicles serve a theological function: they show that God's blessing brings concrete, material results, but the text also warns by recounting Uzziah's downfall when his heart became proud (2 Chron 26:16).
Uzziah also strengthened Jerusalem's defenses and developed war machines, including catapults invented by engineers, which were placed on the towers and corners of the wall (2 Chron 26:15).

footnotes.text: The database number 3007500 represents the biblical figure 307,500, found in 2 Chron 26:13. The discrepancy is due to internal numbering within the database.
King Uzziah (also called Azariah) reigned over Judah for about 52 years (c. 792–740 BC) and was one of the longest-reigning kings. His reign represented one of Judah's most prosperous periods.
The 2,600 family heads who led the army (2 Chron 26:12) formed the command structure. With 307,500 soldiers, this averages about 118 men per family head.

The detailed military figures in Chronicles serve a theological function: they show that God's blessing brings concrete, material results, but the text also warns by recounting Uzziah's downfall when his heart became proud and he entered the temple to burn incense, which was reserved for the priests (2 Chron 26:16–20).

Uzziah also strengthened Jerusalem's defenses and developed war machines, including catapults invented by engineers, which were placed on the towers and corners of the wall (2 Chron 26:15). Archaeological excavations in Judah's fortified cities from this period have revealed evidence of extensive fortification work.
